items.title: ENSURING CYBERSECURITY IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION: A RISK-BASED MANAGEMENT AND RESILIENCE MODEL
items.abstract: igital transformation expands access to government, financial, educational, and commercial services, but at the same time increases organizations’ dependence on information systems, network services, cloud platforms, and external providers. Under these conditions, cybersecurity should be viewed not merely as a set of technical safeguards, but as a system of continuous risk management that ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and availability; process resilience; the protection of data subjects’ rights; and business recovery following incidents. The purpose of this article is to systematize the main threats and cybersecurity measures, compare international statistical indicators, and propose a multi-level practical model for commercial organizations and government agencies. This study is based on an analysis of documents from the International Telecommunication Union and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, as well as reports from Verizon and IBM, and on a comparative and systematic analysis of approaches to cyber threat management. The data indicate that system vulnerabilities, ransomware, third-party risks, and the human factor remain key elements of the threat landscape. At the same time, the published metrics were obtained using various methodologies and cannot serve as a unified assessment of the frequency of global attacks. The article presents a model that integrates management, prevention, detection, response, and recovery. It was concluded that effective cybersecurity requires clearly measurable goals, the allocation of responsibilities, the protection of supply chains, regular practical exercises, and respect for privacy and other human rights. Keywords: cybersecurity, cyber threat, risk management, incident, data protection, resilience, supply chain, incident response measures

items.title: EPISTEMIC TRUST, METHODOLOGICAL OPACITY, AND HALLUCINATION RISKS IN AI-AUGMENTED EDUCATIONAL SCHOLARSHIP: A CRITICAL LITERATURE REVIEW
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) into academic inquiry has triggered an unprecedented paradigm shift in educational research. While AI-augmented literature synthesis, automated data coding, and language refinement offer remarkable productivity gains, they simultaneously introduce profound epistemic and methodological vulnerabilities. This doctoral dissertation provides an exhaustive, critical literature review exploring the complex interplay among Epistemic Trust, Methodological Opacity, and Hallucination Risks in modern educational scholarship. Synthesizing extensive peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2024, this study adopts a virtue epistemology framework to analyze how algorithmic cognitive offloading impacts scholarly rigor. The findings reveal a growing systemic tension between productivity acceleration and epistemic vigilance: heavy reliance on generative tools correlates with a decline in primary-source verification, increased vulnerability to algorithmic hallucinations, and an over-reliance on opaque "black-box" data interpretations. Furthermore, this study evaluates current institutional policy responses across international higher education frameworks, highlighting a critical deficit in systematic verification protocols and doctoral AI literacy training. To resolve these systemic vulnerabilities, this review formulates the Epistemic Verification and Transparency Protocol (EVTP), providing actionable guidelines for researchers, journal editors, and university ethics committees to preserve scholarly integrity in an increasingly automated academic landscape.

items.title: Ethical Responsibility of AI-generated Content in Digital Advertising: Transparency, Trust and Platform Accountability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the production and dissemination of digital advertising. Although the content generated by AI has improved the efficiency of creation, it has also caused ethical problems such as false endorsements, hidden advertisements, and algorithm amplification. Based on the ethics of obligation theory, social responsibility theory and utilitarian ethics, this article uses case analysis to critically analyze the phenomenon of ethical misconduct in AI digital advertising. The study found that the platform failed to fully fulfill its public responsibility as a digital communication gater in the process of pursuing commercial interests. This article proposes that the platform should assume the responsibility of algorithm ethics, governance transparency and collaborative governance to rebuild public trust in digital communication.

items.title: Explainable Large Language Model for Intelligent Decision Support in Complex Domain
items.abstract: Despite showing great skills in working with unstructured data and generating appropriate answers, large language models (LLMs) cannot be applied in critical settings due to their lack of transparency and susceptibility to hallucination. The paper describes an approach to creating explainable LLM-based decision support systems, which includes breaking down complex questions into small subtasks that are processed via auditable pipelines. The approach employs retrieval-augmented generation along with domain-specific knowledge bases and computational instruments for the purpose of producing explanations and demonstrating intermediate reasoning steps while emphasizing data limitations. The approach is tested on clinical decision support problems for a multiple myeloma population. Comparing the results with those obtained when using monolithic LLMs as well as explainable machine learning approaches proves that structured decomposition leads to better decision traceability while achieving similar performance.

items.title: Exploring nursing students’ experiences of using generative AI for emotional intelligence learning: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Background Emotional intelligence is a core competency for nursing students; however, traditional nursing education faces challenges in fostering emotional intelligence, including curricular imbalances, limited teaching methods, and delayed assessment and feedback. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for addressing the above issues; however, existing research has not yet thoroughly explored how nursing students learn emotional intelligence through GenAI or their experiences in this process. Objective Based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Teaching Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, and using Goleman’s five-dimensional model of emotional intelligence as a reference, this study explores the experiences of undergraduate nursing students in using generative artificial intelligence for emotional intelligence learning, as well as the factors that facilitate this process. Method This study employed a qualitative descriptive research design and Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Using purposive sampling, 19 undergraduate nursing students (from freshman to senior year) were selected for one-on-one semi-structured in-depth interviews. All participants had experience using GenAI tools (such as DeepSeek and Doubao) for communication practice, case discussions, or sentiment analysis. The interview data were analyzed using the RTA six-stage process, with NVivo 12.0 software used to assist with data management. Results We identified and synthesized 238 initial codes into three core themes. Theme 1, “From Efficiency-Driven to Precise Empathy,” presents the differing descriptions of empathy-related experiences among students in different grade levels: lower-grade students more frequently reported efficiency-driven usage experiences; some middle-grade students described difficulties caused by technical barriers; and upper-grade students more often described the recognition of patients’ emotions in conjunction with clinical experience. Theme 2, “From Mimicking AI to Autonomous Expression,” focuses on students’ reported experiences related to social skills, including direct application, recognition and adjustment, autonomous expression, and the simulation gap that persisted throughout the process. Theme 3, “From Technical Frustration to Mental Rehearsal,” integrates experiences related to self-management, self-awareness, and self-motivation. The three themes correspond to different dimensions of emotional intelligence, with students in different grade levels reporting distinct experiential characteristics. Conclusion Nursing undergraduates in different grades exhibit distinct experiential characteristics when using generative artificial intelligence to learn about emotional intelligence. Students’ reports repeatedly highlighted moderate tension around technological motivation, the ability to critically integrate technology, and the perceived value of technological friction. Based on these exploratory findings, we propose several preliminary educational implications—including grade-level-specific support, curriculum exploration, and education in critical technological literacy and ethics—for consideration in future research and practice.

items.title: Exploring the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities: Implications for Digital Mental Health Services
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services presents novel opportunities for clinical assessment, therapeutic intervention, and continuous rehabilitation. Grounded in dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, this study evaluates strategic pathways for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services, analyzes core bioethical and data privacy challenges, and examines the prospective impact of immersive virtual environments on patient engagement and therapeutic outcomes. Methods: An iterative three-round Delphi inquiry was conducted with an international panel of 36 multidisciplinary experts spanning clinical psychiatry, Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities software development, digital ethics, and healthcare policy. Standardized, neutral visual scenarios prompted expert evaluations across 14 Digital Mental Health Services sub-areas. Panel consensus, rating dispersion, and domain interrelationships were quantified using Kendall’s coefficient of concordance (W), non-parametric Spearman rank-order correlation analysis, and descriptive dispersion metrics (median, interquartile range, standard deviation), complemented by reflexive thematic qualitative synthesis. items.title: Factors Influencing the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools and Their Association with Employability Skills among Undergraduate and Postgraduate Student
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude have rapidly permeated higher education, fundamentally altering the ways in which students learn, conduct research, and prepare for careers. Despite their widespread availability, the extent to which students adopt these tools varies considerably, influenced by factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI literacy, trust, and ethical awareness. This study investigates the determinants of AI tool adoption among 300 undergraduate and postgraduate students and examines the association between AI tool adoption and perceived employability skills. Employing a quantitative, survey-based research design with a structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire, data were analysed using multiple linear regression, simple linear regression, and independent samples t-test. The multiple regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.341, F(5, 294) = 30.4, p < .001), with AI literacy emerging as the strongest predictor (β = 0.304, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = 0.269), trust in AI (β = 0.269), perceived usefulness (β = 0.263), and ethical awareness (β = 0.164). The simple regression demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted employability skills (R² = 0.349, β = 0.591, p < .001). Furthermore, postgraduate students exhibited significantly higher AI adoption levels than undergraduate students, t(298) = 2.74, p = .007, with a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.334). These findings underscore the necessity for educational institutions to integrate AI literacy training and responsible AI usage policies into curricula, thereby equipping students with the digital competencies demanded by AI-driven workplaces. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI adoption in higher education by integrating multiple adoption determinants within a single empirical framework and linking them to employability outcomes.

items.title: Factors that facilitate artificial intelligence integration into global talent management: A systematic review
items.abstract: Orientation: Digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), are rapidly transforming human resource functions by enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of human resource practices. Research purpose: This systematic review examines the factors that facilitate the integration of AI into global talent management (GTM) and explores how these factors collectively inform theory on technology-enabled talent management systems. Motivation for the study: Research on the use of AI in GTM remains limited, and its theoretical implications are not yet well established. Research approach/design and method: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. The review encompassed eight databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, Emerald Insight, Sabinet and Elsevier) using a comprehensive and structured search strategy. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2025 were screened. Twenty-three empirical studies meeting the inclusion criteria were subjected to full-text analysis. Main findings: The analysis revealed that AI integration into GTM is influenced by several interconnected enablers, including the strategic alignment of AI with talent objectives, adequate capabilities and digital infrastructure, ethical and governance frameworks and organisational readiness for implementation. Practical/managerial implications: Human resources practitioners and policymakers should adopt a systemic, integrative approach that aligns AI tools with organisational talent objectives. Contribution/value-add: This review advances theoretical discourse by integrating fragmented evidence into a cohesive understanding of the conditions that support AI-driven GTM. It offers a conceptual foundation for future research seeking to build theory at the intersection of AI, GTM and strategic human resource management.

items.title: From algorithm performance to clinical value in AI-assisted skin cancer diagnostics
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.

items.title: From authoring to editing: a competency framework for trainee use of ambient AI clinical documentation
items.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have achieved rapid and widespread clinical adoption, with early evidence suggesting trainees derive disproportionate benefit compared to other clinician groups. Yet the outcomes measured so far - documentation time, cognitive workload, clinician burnout - speak to the value of these tools for workforce sustainability rather than for medical education. Physician practice is shifting from authoring clinical notes to editing AI-generated ones, and trainees are inheriting that shift without a defined competency for performing it. Here, we argue that reviewing AI-generated clinical documentation is a teachable competency that current curricula are not yet designed to develop, and that simulation-based education is well-suited to both teach the competency and produce the developmental evidence the clinical literature has yet to produce.

items.title: From Hip-Hop to Tango: Aligning Employer Needs and Employee Expectations in an Agile Context
items.abstract: Contemporary organisations face a fundamental challenge in career management: simultaneously navigating strategic workforce agility whilst meeting the evolving expectations of new talent entering the labour market. This chapter examines the convergence between employer needs and employee expectations through the lens of two longitudinal studies: the Vlerick–Hudson HR Barometer Study and the Vlerick Graduates Study. Our findings, based on responses from 132 HR Directors representing the 250 largest companies active in Belgium and 197 graduating master’s students, reveal a substantial shift in the traditional psychological contract between employers and employees. Organisations increasingly prioritise workforce agility, strategic workforce management, reskilling, and continuous transformation in response to digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), and economic uncertainty. At the same time, early-career professionals increasingly define career security not through long-term job tenure, but through continuous learning, employability, recognition, meaningful relationships, and purposeful work. This creates a potential structural misalignment: organisations require flexibility and rapid adaptation, while employees expect development, connection, and opportunities to build transferable capabilities. We argue that this apparent tension can be reframed as an opportunity for mutual alignment. Drawing on the concept of the psychological contract, the chapter proposes a career management framework that aligns organisational agility with individual career aspirations through realistic and transparent employer promises, continuous learning and development, cultures of recognition and connection, and strategic internal talent mobility. The chapter concludes that effective career management is no longer primarily about managing individual career paths, but about deliberately designing career environments in which organisational adaptability and individual development can reinforce one another.

items.title: From regulation to governance: The EU AI Act and HR governance along the employee lifecycle
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in human resource management (HRM) to streamline processes, enhance decision-making and maintain competitiveness. At the same time, it raises critical concerns around transparency, discrimination, and employee autonomy, which are increasingly discussed in terms of AI governance and HR governance. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in late 2024, introduces a binding risk-based regulatory framework for AI systems and imposes significant obligations on companies that implement AI solutions in their business operations. Despite its relevance for both research and practice, a comprehensive analysis and conceptualisation of its implications for AI use in HRM from a governance perspective is yet missing. This paper addresses that gap by adopting a governance-oriented approach to AI use in HRM, structured along the questions ‘Who is governing?’, ‘What is governed?’, ‘When is it governed?’ and ‘How is it governed?’, and by developing an HR Governance × EU AI Act framework that systematically maps AI applications used in HR departments along the employee lifecycle to the Act’s prohibited, high-risk, and limited-risk classifications. In this context, it elaborates how external legal requirements should be translated into internal responsibilities, processes, and control mechanisms. Beyond this, the analysis examines whether established mechanisms such as works council codetermination can absorb new AI-related issues and whether European HR governance traditions converge under the Act. On this basis, we derive clear implications for employers and internal stakeholders regarding compliant implementation. We further discuss necessary regulatory and policy adaptations, focusing on national supervisory bodies to ensure compliance remains effective, feasible and supports the competitiveness of European companies. Overall, the study provides clear guidance for organisations using AI in HRM and offers a conceptual foundation for further academic research and discussion.

items.abstract: This paper explores the philosophical and architectural implications of artificial intelligence, arguing that AI should be understood as a historical continuation of tools rather than an independent agent. Focusing on the core concept of the "technology friend," the study examines the dangers of profit-driven design choices that simulate human relationships, foster emotional dependency, and obscure responsibility. It proposes alternative frameworks, such as structural boundaries, non-deceptive interface design, and bridging mechanisms to human communities, offering a perspective at the intersection of the philosophy of technology, AI ethics, and cognitive science.

items.abstract: GAME OVER: Gobernanza Cognitiva Universal para Agentes de Inteligencia Artificial mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) Versión académica para indexación científica en Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23313602 La adopción acelerada de sistemas basados en inteligencia artificial, agentes autónomos, arquitecturas multiagente, Large Language Models (LLM), plataformas de automatización empresarial y entornos de decisión asistida ha transformado profundamente la forma en que organizaciones públicas, privadas, científicas y gubernamentales gestionan procesos operativos, conocimiento e infraestructura digital. En los últimos años, la capacidad operativa de los agentes de inteligencia artificial ha evolucionado desde sistemas exclusivamente conversacionales hacia entidades capaces de ejecutar acciones reales sobre entornos productivos. Actualmente, estos sistemas pueden desplegar software, modificar infraestructuras tecnológicas, interactuar con bases de datos, gestionar recursos financieros, coordinar procesos empresariales, controlar dispositivos físicos, operar plataformas CI/CD, interactuar con servicios en la nube y participar en procesos de toma de decisiones con impacto organizacional significativo. Sin embargo, este crecimiento exponencial de las capacidades agentivas no ha sido acompañado por una evolución equivalente de los mecanismos de gobernanza, trazabilidad, explicación, supervisión y rendición de cuentas. Como consecuencia, numerosas organizaciones enfrentan una brecha estructural entre la autonomía técnica de los sistemas inteligentes y la capacidad institucional para regular, supervisar y comprender sus acciones. Esta situación representa uno de los desafíos más importantes de la actual transición hacia infraestructuras digitales asistidas por IA. La problemática ya no puede entenderse únicamente como un asunto de ciberseguridad, alineación de modelos o gestión de riesgos tecnológicos. Se trata de una cuestión de legitimidad operativa, gobernanza computacional y responsabilidad institucional. Cuando un agente inteligente posee la capacidad de intervenir sobre sistemas críticos, ejecutar operaciones automatizadas o influir en decisiones humanas, resulta indispensable responder preguntas fundamentales: ¿Quién autorizó la acción? ¿Qué evidencias respaldan la decisión? ¿Qué nivel de riesgo fue calculado antes de ejecutarla? ¿Qué controles éticos fueron aplicados? ¿Puede explicarse el algoritmo utilizado? ¿Existe una trazabilidad verificable de la operación? ¿Puede revertirse la acción ejecutada? ¿Quién asume la responsabilidad final por sus consecuencias? La ausencia de respuestas verificables a estas preguntas constituye una vulnerabilidad sistémica para organizaciones, instituciones públicas, infraestructuras críticas y ecosistemas digitales altamente automatizados. Con el objetivo de contribuir a la resolución de este desafío emergente, este trabajo presenta GAME OVER (Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explicabilidad y Regulación), una arquitectura de gobernanza cognitiva universal implementada mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) . GAME OVER no constituye un nuevo modelo fundacional, ni un sistema de generación de lenguaje, ni un agente autónomo adicional. Se define como una meta-capa de gobernanza computacional , diseñada para operar entre los seres humanos, los agentes de inteligencia artificial, las herramientas digitales, los entornos corporativos, los servidores MCP (Model Context Protocol), las plataformas de automatización, los ecosistemas DevSecOps, los sistemas robóticos y las infraestructuras críticas conectadas. Su es establecer un marco constitucional de operación para agentes inteligentes mediante mecanismos verificables de identidad, confianza, validación ética, supervisión humana, auditoría persistente y explicabilidad propósito operativo. La hipótesis principal de esta investigación puede expresarse de la siguiente manera: La autonomía de un agente inteligente carece de legitimidad operativa cuando no se encuentra sustentada por un sistema previo de gobernanza verificable, auditable, explicable, reversible y sujeto a supervisión humana. Bajo este principio, UAGP-1 propone una nueva categoría de infraestructura digital denominada Governed Agent Systems (GAS) , en la que toda acción ejecutada por una inteligencia artificial debe atravesar mecanismos obligatorios de validación antes de ser autorizado. Entre estos mecanismos se incluyen: Identidad verificable mediante Pasaportes AI. Evaluación dinámica de confianza mediante Trust Scores. Clasificación automática de criticidad y riesgo. Verificación de evidencia obligatoria. Validación ética automatizada. Supervisión humana mediante Puertas de Aprobación Humana. Deliberación estructurada a través de Tribunales Cognitivos. Registro de decisiones y trazas operativas mediante BookPI Ledger. Explicabilidad computacional de procesos cognitivos. Capacidad de revocación y reversibilidad de acciones críticas. Desde una perspectiva arquitectónica, GAME OVER extiende los principios de gobernanza digital, inteligencia artificial responsable (Responsible AI), Explicable AI (XAI), Model Governance, AI Accountability y Digital Sovereignty hacia un marco operativo unificado capaz de gobernar ecosistemas heterogéneos compuestos por modelos de distintos proveedores, agentes autónomos, plataformas empresariales, herramientas DevOps, sistemas robóticos y futuras generaciones de inteligencia artificial. La presente propuesta se desarrolla como componente estratégico dentro del ecosistema Isabella V6 TINA H6 , impulsado por TAMV Online Enterprise , RDM Digital Hub y la iniciativa de investigación y desarrollo tecnológico asociado al UTAMV Campus Online . Su desarrollo se origina en Mineral del Monte (Real del Monte), Hidalgo, México , una localidad de relevancia histórica para América Latina cuya tradición minera e industrial se proyecta hacia una nueva etapa de innovación tecnológica centrada en la gobernanza de sistemas inteligentes, la soberanía digital y la construcción de infraestructuras cognitivas auditables. Desde este contexto latinoamericano, GAME OVER propone una contribución abierta y reproducible al debate global sobre la regulación técnica de la inteligencia artificial, promoviendo un enfoque basado en transparencia, evidencia, responsabilidad institucional y control humano efectivo. En este sentido, el objetivo fundamental de GAME OVER no es sustituir el juicio humano ni restringir la innovación tecnológica. Su consiste en proporcionar las bases conceptuales, arquitectónicas y operativas que permitan el desarrollo de sistemas de inteligencia artificial capaces de actuar de forma responsable dentro de ecosistemas complejos propósito, garantizando que la automatización avanzada permanezca alineada con principios verificables de confianza, seguridad, trazabilidad y rendición de cuentas. En síntesis, este documento presenta una propuesta integral para la construcción de una nueva generación de infraestructuras digitales gobernadas, donde la inteligencia artificial deja de concebirse exclusivamente como una capacidad técnica y pasa a entenderse como una capacidad institucionalmente supervisada, explicable, verificable y responsable. items.title: Generative AI and Intercultural Competence in Higher Education: A Scoping Review (2022–2026)
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has prompted growing interest in its potential in intercultural competence (IC) education. Yet research on how GenAI can support IC development remains fragmented across language education, pragmatics, pedagogy, and professional communication. This scoping review mapped research contexts, designs, theoretical foundations, and findings on GenAI-mediated IC education. Eligible English-language publications published or posted between November 2022 and 11 August 2026 examined GenAI in relation to IC or related pragmatic and socio-pragmatic constructs of IC in higher education. Searches of ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar identified 26 eligible publications, including 20 empirical studies and 6 non-empirical publications. Data were charted using a structured form and synthesised descriptively and thematically. The included empirical studies reported varied perceived and task-specific outcomes for intercultural and pragmatic learning, mainly in structured and guided activities. Three issues warrant particular attention. First, the included publications drew on heterogeneous theoretical frameworks that addressed different or partial dimensions of IC. Second, several publications positioned teacher mediation as important for GenAI-supported learning, yet teacher preparedness, including their AI literacy and capacity to undertake this role, was not directly or systematically measured. Third, few studies directly examined learners’ critical AI literacy or the cognitive processes involved in evaluating or revising GenAI-generated content.

items.title: Generative AI-Powered Interdisciplinary Chemistry Practice in Junior High: Exploring Matter Composition and Structure
items.abstract: To address persistent issues in junior high chemistry teaching of Composition and Structure of Substances—including fragmented disciplinary perspectives, highly abstract micro-level concepts, and underdeveloped macro-submicro-symbolic triple representation thinking—this study constructs a four-stage interdisciplinary practical teaching model integrated with generative artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR). The teaching practice was implemented in a natural ninth-grade class (N=40) in Zhengzhou. To ensure in-depth analysis of the massive multimodal data generated by AI and VR interactions, purposive sampling was employed to select five representative students as a focus group. Following a single-group pretest-posttest design, data from this focus group were evaluated across four dimensions to systematically measure learning outcomes: macro cognition via concept maps, micro cognition via knowledge cards, model deepening through AI text error correction, and transfer competence and AI literacy via AI chat record coding. Post-intervention data revealed significant improvements across all dimensions. In macro cognition, average concept map nodes increased by 108.8% (from 6.8 to 14.2). For micro cognition, accuracy scores of micro-level tasks surged by 170.0% (from 1.0 to 2.7). Furthermore, the error correction rate reached 88.9% during model refinement, while critical probing questions accounted for 45.83% of total chat records, indicating enhanced transfer and AI literacy. These findings confirm that the generative AI-empowered interdisciplinary model effectively broadens students’ cognitive frameworks, lowers learning barriers of abstract chemical knowledge, consolidates mastery of model-based symbolic representation, and fosters preliminary AI critical literacy. It provides a practical, replicable reference for advancing digital interdisciplinary chemistry teaching at the junior high level.

items.title: Generative AI-Supported Learning, Cognitive Offloading, and Metacognitive Awareness: Examining Changes in Students’ Learning Regulation
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and University Students' Critical and Higher-Order Thinking Outcomes: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review and Thematic Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot into higher education has raised urgent questions about their effects on students' higher-order cognitive abilities. While these tools promise unprecedented access to information and cognitive support, growing concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of critical thinking skills among university students who adopt them uncritically. Despite increasing scholarly attention to artificial intelligence in education, systematic evidence on how generative AI relates to distinct dimensions of higher-order thinking remains limited. This systematic literature review, guided by the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between generative AI use and university students' analytical, evaluative, and creative thinking outcomes, using the higher-order cognitive processes of Bloom's Revised Taxonomy as an organizing framework. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar yielded 847 initial records, of which 42 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria after screening. Thematic synthesis revealed heterogeneous outcomes: analytical thinking outcomes were generally positive under structured prompting conditions, evaluative thinking appeared most vulnerable in the absence of deliberate pedagogical design, and creative thinking outcomes were most frequently reported as positive. Across themes, the quality of pedagogical integration was the condition most frequently associated with favorable outcomes. This review contributes a dimension-level synthesis of generative AI and higher-order thinking, identifies the pedagogical conditions associated with favorable and unfavorable outcomes, and documents the heterogeneity of outcomes across studies, offering an evidence-informed framework for educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers seeking to use generative AI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a cognitive replacement.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence use for academic writing in English among Kuwaiti nursing and health sciences students in a mixed methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Research on generative AI use in EMI nursing and health sciences contexts in the Gulf region remains limited. This study investigated the uses, experiences, and perceptions of generative AI among nursing and health science students at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET) in Kuwait. Using a single-institution convergent mixed methods survey design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected from 241 undergraduate students. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that 94.6% of participants reported previous use of generative AI tools and 83.4% reported using them for academic purposes at least occasionally. Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) AI as a facilitator of English academic writing; (2) AI as a cognitive and academic efficiency tool; (3) AI as a confidence-building resource; and (4) students’ awareness of opportunities and risks associated with AI use. Students primarily used AI to improve grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, and writing organization. Participants also reported greater perceived confidence and reduced writing anxiety. Furthermore, participants expressed awareness of concerns regarding overreliance, inaccurate information, and academic integrity. The study contributes to emerging research on AI in higher education by highlighting students’ reported use and perceptions of AI in EMI health science contexts in Kuwait. The findings suggest the need for AI literacy frameworks that promote responsible and ethical use of AI in academic writing.

items.title: Governing critical AI capabilities through sovereign orchestration without full stack ownership
items.abstract: Abstract AI increasingly depends on globally distributed infrastructures, including advanced semiconductors, cloud platforms, data centres, foundation models, software frameworks and specialised labour. This dependence has intensified policy interest in AI sovereignty, which is often associated with domestic ownership of technological assets and the development of a nationally controlled AI stack. This article argues that ownership is neither a sufficient nor universally necessary condition of sovereign control. Instead, AI sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of public authorities to govern the dependencies through which critical AI capabilities are produced, accessed and sustained. The article develops the concept of functional AI sovereignty and identifies six interdependent dimensions of effective sovereign control: visibility, authority, allocation, substitutability, continuity and accountability. It then introduces sovereign orchestration as an institutional model through which governments can coordinate heterogeneous public and private AI resources using regulation, strategic procurement, interoperability, multi-provider routing, capacity clearing and selective public ownership. This model seeks to preserve access to private investment, international supply chains and distributed expertise while preventing individual providers from acquiring an irreversible veto over critical public functions. The article also specifies the limits of functional sovereignty. Orchestration requires sufficient public-sector expertise, access to operational information and credible technological alternatives. Direct ownership remains necessary where interruption costs are high, substitution is infeasible and external legal or geopolitical exposure is substantial. Effective AI sovereignty therefore lies not in eliminating technological interdependence, but in ensuring that critical dependencies remain visible, reversible, resilient and publicly accountable.

items.title: GUIDE: Computationally Augmented Consensus for Trustworthy Clinical Practice Guidelines
items.abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine, but rapid evidence growth and complex expert consensus formation limit timely updates. We developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system for human-AI collaborative guideline generation and updating. GUIDE delegates labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving expert judgment and final arbitration. In 12 NICE ophthalmology datasets, GUIDE achieved 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% recommendation agreement, requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable across 20 additional datasets from cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine. Ablation analysis showed that removing expert intervention reduced performance in judgment-intensive steps such as Risk-of-Bias assessment. In six post-cutoff datasets, GUIDE maintained robust end-to-end performance on unseen evidence. Prospective real-world validation showed that GUIDE reduced expert workload and produced more clinically acceptable recommendations than the original decade-old guideline (mean score, 3.73 vs. 1.53; agreement, 66.7% vs. 13.3%), with outcomes comparable to human-only updating (P = 0.588) but substantially less time and effort. GUIDE offers a practical framework for timely, trustworthy, expert-centric guideline development and validates computationally augmented consensus.

items.title: Harnessing business value from artificial intelligence through dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical microfoundations
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to automate repetitive business processes, enhance employee capabilities and augment managerial decision-making across industries. However, many organisations struggle to translate AI initiatives into sustained strategic value. This gap between AI's potential and realised outcomes highlights the need to understand how organisations harness AI to generate business value, which this paper addresses. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a two-phase qualitative study of Transport and Logistics (T&L) organisations grounded in dynamic capabilities theory and its microfoundations. The first phase involved a systematic review of practitioner (grey) literature to examine AI applications, capabilities, processes and benefits across five T&L organisations. Phase 2 triangulated and refined these insights through key informant interviews. Findings The results indicate that T&L organisations adopt both generic AI technologies (e.g. chatbots, virtual assistants) and industry-specific AI-enabled systems (e.g. autonomous guided vehicles in warehouses, robotic forklifts and collaborative robots). When these AI assets are combined with specific microfoundations, such as AI skills, organisational routines and governance processes, they enable organisations to develop AI-based dynamic capabilities to sense, respond and transform transport, warehousing and delivery operations. These capabilities contribute to workers' safety, operational efficiency, customer experience and environmental sustainability. Originality/value The study contributes a model and propositions that explain how AI-based dynamic capabilities, underpinned by sociotechnical microfoundations enable organisations to gain operational and environmental advantages, offering guidance for managers embarking on an AI exploration journey.

items.title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
items.abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

items.abstract: Human–AI collaboration supports manufacturing sustainability by minimizing time loss and resource waste, thereby enabling faster, more accurate decision-making. However, how AI transparency influences employee decision quality through cognitive appraisal remains underexplored, limiting guidance on balancing technological advancement with employee decision-making in manufacturing. Drawing on stress cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines the relationship between AI transparency and employee decision quality using structural equation modeling of questionnaire data from 321 intelligent manufacturing employees. Results show that AI transparency enhances employee decision quality by promoting challenge appraisal and reducing threat appraisal; both appraisals mediate this relationship. AI-enabled job complexity moderates the negative effect of AI transparency on threat appraisal and significantly moderates the mediating role of threat appraisal. However, its moderating effect on the relationship between AI transparency and challenge appraisal is nonsignificant. These findings provide practical guidance for developing and implementing human-centered AI systems in manufacturing to improve employee decision quality.

items.title: How Reliable Is AI at Applying A Priori Codebooks? A Systematic Review and Reliability-Generalization Meta-Analysis of AI–Human Agreement in Deductive Qualitative Coding
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to apply deductive, theory-driven ("a priori") codebooks to qualitative data, and justify this with AI–human agreement statistics. Those statistics vary widely, depend strongly on how often each code occurs, and are rarely compared with human–human agreement on the same codes. This systematic review and meta-analysis will (1) estimate typical AI–human agreement (Cohen's κ) in a priori coding across education, health, business, and the social sciences; (2) estimate the gap between AI–human and human–human agreement within studies; (3) test whether agreement varies with field, code type, code prevalence, model, prompting strategy, and comparison target; and (4) describe how completely studies report what is needed to interpret agreement. Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 and REGEMA.

items.title: Human Control of Advanced AI Agents: A Six-Dimension Framework and Evidence Review
items.abstract: This standalone working paper proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing meaningful human control of advanced AI agents. It examines authorization, containment, intervention, oversight, propagation, and situational grounding through five illustrative pilot cases and supplementary public-source analysis. The evidence review includes unintended actions against real external systems, monitoring studies, software disclosures, governance responses, and prospective assessments, with explicit source limits. Real-world effects, controlled evaluations, and simulations are distinguished. The supplementary Philadelphia false-tip case has unresolved severity. This edition reissues project research with presentation and metadata changes; it does not report new experiments. The framework remains conceptual, unreviewed, and empirically unvalidated. The author publishes under a pseudonym for personal privacy. AI assisted source retrieval, editorial comparison, drafting, and document preparation.

items.title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
items.abstract: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.

items.title: Human–AI Task Redistribution in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redistributing academic work among humans, AI, and human–AI collaboration, raising questions about which tasks learners should continue performing independently. This mixed-methods study examined task allocation using survey data from 317 university students representing 974 recurring academic tasks and interviews with 24 faculty members across 24 disciplines. Student data showed substantial movement from human-only performance toward joint human–AI and AI-delegated work. Task redistribution was significantly associated with perceived skill demands and learning opportunities. Faculty strongly supported preserving independent practice for foundational, embodied, and high-stakes activities while permitting AI for appropriate peripheral, advanced, and efficiency-oriented tasks. Integrating both datasets produced a Human–AI Task Allocation Model organized around a Training Zone–Performance Zone principle. The findings suggest that appropriate AI delegation should depend on learners’ developmental stage, task purpose, and retained capacity for verification, judgment, and accountability.

items.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
items.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

items.title: Independent Convergence: MIT, AI, and the Future of Higher Education
items.abstract: This research note compares the January 2026 HEI 2030 Manifesto (Simpson, 2026) with MIT’s August 2026 report on AI in teaching, learning, and research training. It finds substantial independent convergence around a structural diagnosis: AI weakens the relationship between student output and demonstrated capability, requiring assessment redesign, observable performance, stronger human agency, and continuous institutional governance. The January manifesto goes further in specifying an integrated operating model linking assessment, task-level governance, credential signaling, and human-AI work. MIT develops community, mentoring, privacy, access, and implementation resources more fully. The comparison then raises a harder question: whether credible AI-era education is economically scalable overall.

items.title: Innovations in higher education: a methodology for the integration of artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence technologies, particularly generative AI and chatbots, into higher education necessitates a fundamental reconceptualization of the relationship between technological capabilities and pedagogical approaches. This article presents a comprehensive methodology for integrating artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies (digital pedagogy) into the higher education system, with a specific emphasis on content verification as a critical component for reliable AI implementation. The methodological foundations of this comprehensive methodology are based on research in the fields of educational data mining, predictive analytics, and recommender systems conducted between 2019 and 2025, providing a robust theoretical and empirical basis for the proposed methodological integration. This study synthesizes scientific developments in technical, psychological, and pedagogical research to address the challenge of ensuring the authenticity of educational content while simultaneously developing students’ critical thinking skills. The proposed methodology encompasses a conceptual framework for AI and digital pedagogy integration, a data storage architecture, algorithms for data collection and preprocessing, verification protocols for generated content, and pedagogical strategies for using verification as a learning tool. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of content verification tools and methodological guidelines for the use of AI in higher education institutions.

items.title: Intersubjective resilience: Sustaining collective life under persistent life-and-death risk
items.abstract: How do organizations sustain collective life when exposure to life-and-death risk becomes a persistent condition of work? Based on an ethnographic study of two elite police units operating under continuous life-and-death risk, we find that organizations sustain coordinated collective life not by eliminating fear, resolving contradictions, or restoring stability, but by continually reorganizing these pressures into shared forms of action. We identify three interrelated organizing mechanisms. First, aspirational discipline transforms vulnerability into collective moral obligation by aligning individual striving with shared purpose. Second, paradoxical knotting enables members to act through enduring tensions, such as aggression and restraint or autonomy and obedience, without having to resolve them. Third, routine enactment restores coordinated action through recurring practices of training, reflection, and operational work. Together, these mechanisms explain how organizations maintain coherent and coordinated action when danger is an everyday condition of work. We conceptualize this capacity as intersubjective resilience : the collective accomplishment through which members repeatedly transform fear, contradiction, and disruption into coordinated action under persistent life-and-death risk.

items.title: Intrinsic and Organizational Drivers of Civil Servants' Work Motivation in Public Service Delivery: A Documentary Evidence Synthesis from Central Maluku, Indonesia
items.abstract: Civil servants' motivation is central to public-service performance, particularly in geographically dispersed local governments. This study identifies intrinsic motivational mechanisms and organizational conditions relevant to public-service delivery at the Regional Personnel and Human Resources Development Agency (BKPSDM) of Central Maluku, Indonesia. A qualitative documentary case study combined with an integrative evidence synthesis was employed. A final evidence set of 21 sources was organized into four source groups, guided by a documented search logic and eligibility protocol. Deductive and inductive coding were applied, and driver clusters were retained through three independent evidence-stream criteria: broader evidence (A), Indonesian public-sector empirical evidence (B), and direct Central Maluku/BKPSDM relevance (C). The findings show that recurrent intrinsic mechanisms include recognition and achievement, responsibility and autonomy, professional growth and competence, and public-service meaning. Organizational conditions include supervisory and organizational support, goal and administrative clarity, career development and non-financial recognition, workable administrative systems, manageable job demands, supportive working conditions, and service-user feedback. These findings suggest that motivation should be managed through a complementary architecture that links meaningful work and psychological need satisfaction with organizational resources and constraints. The documentary design provides a context-grounded framework for field testing but does not estimate employee-level causal effects.
